interview.question: How do nodeSelector and node affinity differ?
interview.answer: nodeSelector matches node labels and requires all specified labels. Node affinity is more expressive and supports both hard and soft scheduling rules.
interview.followUp: How would you combine them? Both are evaluated, so a node must satisfy the nodeSelector and the node-affinity requirements.

interview.question: What are the two node-affinity rule types?
interview.answer: requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution prevents scheduling unless the rule matches. preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution makes the scheduler try matching nodes, but it can schedule elsewhere if necessary.
interview.followUp: What does IgnoredDuringExecution imply? A later label change does not make this rule a requirement to evict the already-running Pod according to this scheduling rule.

interview.question: Where is node affinity declared and how is it expressed?
interview.answer: Node affinity is configured under `.spec.affinity.nodeAffinity`. Its selector terms use node-label match expressions, allowing more detailed selection logic than nodeSelector.
interview.followUp: How can you express alternatives? Use nodeSelectorTerms and match expressions to describe the accepted node-label combinations.

keyPoints: Use nodeSelector for straightforward placement based on a set of required node labels.
A Pod declares its basic node-label requirements in `spec.nodeSelector`.
Choose affinity when placement needs richer matching logic than exact label pairs.
Node affinity selects eligible nodes by evaluating labels attached to those nodes.
Required node affinity acts as a hard filter: an unmatched rule leaves the Pod unscheduled.
Preferred node affinity influences the scheduler's choice among otherwise eligible nodes.
gotchas: Combining nodeSelector with node affinity narrows eligibility because the Pod must satisfy both sets of constraints.
Preferred node affinity is a soft preference, not a guarantee; the scheduler may use another eligible node.
Every nodeSelector label is mandatory, so a missing label prevents the Pod from landing on that node.

Scheduling & resources::Pod disruption b.summary: A PodDisruptionBudget limits simultaneous Pod unavailability caused by voluntary disruptions. It protects a selected replicated application by requiring a minimum available level or allowing only a maximum unavailable level.
Scheduling & resources::Pod disruption b.explanation: A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) applies to Pods selected by labels and limits voluntary evictions so the selected replicated workload retains its availability requirement. Set exactly one of minAvailable or maxUnavailable; the value may be a number or percentage. Eviction requests are admitted only when the resulting availability still satisfies the budget.
Scheduling & resources::Pod disruption b.syntax:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: <labels>
  minAvailable: <number-or-percentage>
  # or maxUnavailable: <number-or-percentage>

parameters.name: spec.selector
parameters.description: Required label selector identifying the Pods covered by the budget.

parameters.name: spec.minAvailable
parameters.description: Minimum number or percentage of selected Pods that must remain available after an eviction; mutually exclusive with maxUnavailable.

parameters.name: spec.maxUnavailable
parameters.description: Maximum number or percentage of selected Pods that may be unavailable after an eviction; mutually exclusive with minAvailable.

Scheduling & resources::Pod disruption b.returns: An admission decision for a voluntary eviction: allowed when the resulting selected-Pod availability satisfies the PDB, otherwise blocked or delayed.

example.title: Require two available Pods
example.code:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: web-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
example.explanation: This budget requires two selected web Pods to remain available after a voluntary eviction.

useCases.title: Keep enough replicas running while nodes are drained.
useCases.scenario: Planned node maintenance

useCases.title: Prevent voluntary evictions from removing too many members for quorum.
useCases.scenario: Quorum-based services

useCases.title: Set a count or percentage that reflects the application's availability tolerance.
useCases.scenario: Highly available replicated applications

interview.question: What does a PodDisruptionBudget protect?
interview.answer: A PDB limits simultaneous Pod loss caused by voluntary disruption. It does so by requiring a minimum available count or by limiting the maximum unavailable count for Pods matched by its selector.
interview.followUp: What happens when a node drain would violate the budget? The Eviction API refuses or delays that eviction until the budget can be satisfied.

interview.question: How does a PDB choose the Pods it governs?
interview.answer: The selector identifies the Pods covered by the budget. The PDB then evaluates the selected Pods' availability after a proposed eviction, even accounting for the evicted Pod's absence.
interview.followUp: Why should a selector be narrow and intentional? An overly broad selector can make unrelated workloads share one disruption budget and unnecessarily block evictions.

interview.question: Do PDBs control every kind of Pod disruption?
interview.answer: PDBs govern voluntary evictions, while rolling-update availability is controlled by the workload resource's update strategy. Involuntary disruptions are not prevented, but they count against the budget.
interview.followUp: How can unhealthy Pods affect draining? The documentation recommends the AlwaysAllow unhealthy-pod eviction policy so misbehaving applications can still be evicted during a node drain.

keyPoints: Use a PDB to cap simultaneous voluntary availability loss for a replicated application.
Express the policy relative to the workload's intended replica count.
For five intended replicas and four required available, one voluntary eviction is allowed but a second is not.
gotchas: Some voluntary actions, including directly deleting Pods or Deployments, can bypass a PDB; tools should use the Eviction API.
A PDB cannot stop failures or other involuntary unavailability, although those unavailable Pods reduce the remaining budget.

Scheduling & resources::Quality of servi.summary: Kubernetes QoS classes help determine which Pods are most likely to be evicted when a node is under resource pressure. The usual order is BestEffort, Burstable, then Guaranteed, refined by resource usage and Pod priority.
Scheduling & resources::Quality of servi.explanation: Kubernetes assigns each Pod a QoS class from its container resource requests and limits. During node-pressure eviction, the kubelet generally considers BestEffort Pods first, then Burstable Pods, and finally Guaranteed Pods; however, actual ranking also considers whether usage exceeds requests, Pod priority, and usage relative to requests.

example.title: Guaranteed QoS Pod
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: qos-demo
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.27
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: "100m"
        memory: "128Mi"
      limits:
        cpu: "100m"
        memory: "128Mi"
example.explanation: This Pod qualifies for the Guaranteed QoS class because its CPU and memory requests equal its limits.

useCases.title: Protect important workloads
useCases.scenario: Protect critical workloads from node-pressure eviction by assigning matching CPU and memory requests and limits.

useCases.title: Predict eviction risk
useCases.scenario: Estimate which Pods a pressured node may terminate when capacity is exhausted.

useCases.title: Investigate evictions
useCases.scenario: Diagnose unexpected evictions by comparing Pod QoS, requests, limits, priority, and actual usage.

interview.question: What are the Kubernetes QoS classes, and what is their usual eviction order?
interview.answer: Kubernetes defines Guaranteed, Burstable, and BestEffort QoS classes. Under node resource pressure, the usual eviction order is BestEffort, then Burstable, then Guaranteed.
interview.followUp: What can change the apparent order? The kubelet also considers whether usage exceeds requests, Pod priority, and usage relative to requests.

interview.question: How does Kubernetes classify a Pod as Guaranteed?
interview.answer: A Pod is Guaranteed when every container has positive CPU and memory requests and limits, and each request equals its corresponding limit. If these conditions are not met but at least one relevant request or limit exists, the Pod may be Burstable.
interview.followUp: How does a Pod become BestEffort? It has no CPU or memory requests or limits for any container.

interview.question: How does node-pressure eviction differ from scheduler preemption?
interview.answer: Node-pressure eviction is performed by the kubelet to reclaim resources when a node is under pressure. Scheduler preemption is different: it removes lower-priority Pods so a pending higher-priority Pod can be scheduled, and QoS is not used to select those preemption targets.
interview.followUp: Which signal does node-pressure eviction use first? Whether usage of the starved resource exceeds the Pod's request.

keyPoints: Every Pod receives one of three QoS classes: Guaranteed, Burstable, or BestEffort.
The broad eviction sequence under node pressure is BestEffort first, Burstable second, and Guaranteed last.
For resource-pressure eviction, Pods that stay within their resource requests are not candidates on that basis.
The kubelet refines the broad QoS order using resource-request overuse, Pod priority, and usage compared with requests.
A Pod's effective request is calculated by adding the requests of its containers.
BestEffort Pods receive the least protection from node-pressure eviction.
gotchas: A Pod can still be evicted when it exceeds its resource request during node pressure, even if its QoS class is otherwise relatively protected.
Do not confuse node-pressure eviction with scheduler preemption: preemption chooses targets using priority, not QoS.
When a Pod becomes an eviction candidate because of resource pressure, eviction terminates every container in that Pod.

Scheduling & resources::Requests and lim.sourceTitle: Resource Management for Pods and Containers | Kubernetes
Scheduling & resources::Requests and lim.summary: Use CPU and memory requests to reserve capacity and guide Pod placement; use limits to cap what a container can consume at runtime.
Scheduling & resources::Requests and lim.explanation: A container's requests describe the CPU and memory capacity the scheduler uses when selecting a node, while limits define the maximum resources the running container may consume. The kubelet reserves at least the requested amount for that container and enforces limits; if a limit is supplied without a request, Kubernetes uses the limit as the request unless a default was applied.
Scheduling & resources::Requests and lim.syntax:
spec.containers[].resources:
  requests:
    cpu: <quantity>
    memory: <quantity>
  limits:
    cpu: <quantity>
    memory: <quantity>

parameters.name: spec.containers[].resources.requests.cpu
parameters.description: CPU amount requested for scheduling and reservation.

parameters.name: spec.containers[].resources.requests.memory
parameters.description: Memory amount requested for scheduling and reservation.

parameters.name: spec.containers[].resources.limits.cpu
parameters.description: Maximum CPU amount the container may consume.

parameters.name: spec.containers[].resources.limits.memory
parameters.description: Maximum memory amount the container may consume.

example.title: Declare container requests and limits
example.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: resource-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx:1.27
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "250m"
          memory: "128Mi"
        limits:
          cpu: "500m"
          memory: "256Mi"
example.explanation: This Pod reserves a quarter CPU and 128 MiB of memory for scheduling, while allowing the container to use up to half a CPU and 256 MiB.

useCases.title: Ensure a Pod is scheduled only where its declared CPU and memory fit.
useCases.scenario: Reliable placement

useCases.title: Prevent a container from consuming more CPU or memory than its configured ceiling.
useCases.scenario: Runtime containment

useCases.title: Express each container's requirements and derive the Pod's resource totals from them.
useCases.scenario: Multi-container Pods

related: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

interview.question: What is the difference between a resource request and a resource limit?
interview.answer: Requests are the amounts the scheduler uses to decide where a Pod can run. Limits are enforced by the kubelet so the running container cannot use more than the configured amount.
interview.followUp: What happens when only a limit is specified? Kubernetes copies that limit into the request unless an admission-time mechanism has already supplied a default request.

interview.question: How does Kubernetes use requests during scheduling?
interview.answer: The scheduler checks each resource type independently and places a Pod only on a node whose available capacity can accommodate the Pod's resource requests. The request is therefore a scheduling and reservation signal, not simply an application preference.
interview.followUp: How is the Pod-level request calculated? For a given resource, Kubernetes sums the requests of all containers in the Pod.

interview.question: Where are requests and limits declared?
interview.answer: For each container, CPU and memory values are declared under `resources.requests` and `resources.limits`. CPU, memory, ephemeral storage, and huge pages are among the resource types supported by these fields.
interview.followUp: Can requests and limits be specified at Pod scope? Yes; the documentation also describes Pod-level CPU and memory resource fields under `spec.resources`.

keyPoints: A request influences the scheduler's node-placement decision.
A limit is enforced at runtime by the kubelet.
The requested amount is reserved for the individual container.
Resource requirements are configured per container in the Pod specification.
A node must have enough capacity for the aggregate requests of scheduled containers.
gotchas: A limit without an explicit request can become the request automatically, unless admission-time defaults provide one.
Scheduling considers the combined requests of containers in the Pod, not merely one container's values.
A Pod's effective request or limit for a resource is the total across its containers.

Scheduling & resources::Taints and toler.summary: Taints repel pods from nodes unless those pods declare matching tolerations. This lets operators reserve nodes for workloads that explicitly accept them, while placement still depends on other scheduling constraints.
Scheduling & resources::Taints and toler.explanation: A taint marks a node so pods without a matching toleration are rejected according to the taint effect. A toleration on a PodSpec permits matching, but does not force placement there; the scheduler still considers other constraints. Matching uses key and effect plus either Equal with the same value or Exists without a value.
Scheduling & resources::Taints and toler.syntax:
kubectl taint nodes <node-name> <key>=<value>:<effect>
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: <key>
    operator: Equal
    value: <value>
    effect: <effect>

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Taint key used for matching; an empty key matches all keys when operator is Exists.

parameters.name: operator
parameters.description: Matching mode: Equal compares values; Exists matches any value and should omit value.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Taint value matched by Equal; it should be empty with Exists.

parameters.name: effect
parameters.description: Effect to match: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, or NoExecute; empty matches all effects.

parameters.name: tolerationSeconds
parameters.description: For NoExecute, how many seconds the toleration remains effective; omitted means indefinitely.

example.title: Reserve a node for an accepted workload
example.code:
kubectl taint nodes node1 dedicated=team-a:NoSchedule

cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: team-a-workload
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: dedicated
    operator: Equal
    value: team-a
    effect: NoSchedule
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
EOF
example.explanation: The command repels pods from node1 unless they have the matching toleration; the Pod manifest supplies that toleration.

useCases.title: Dedicated nodes
useCases.scenario: Keep general workloads away from nodes reserved for a dedicated team or application.

useCases.title: Specialized hardware
useCases.scenario: Prevent ordinary pods from landing on specialized hardware unless they explicitly support it.

useCases.title: Failure handling
useCases.scenario: Control whether unhealthy-node taints merely block new placement or also remove existing pods.

interview.question: What is the difference between a taint and a toleration?
interview.answer: A taint is placed on a node and repels pods that do not tolerate it. A toleration is placed in the PodSpec and allows the pod to schedule when it matches the taint; it does not require placement on that node.
interview.followUp: How is a taint matched? The keys and effects must match, then either Exists is used without a value or Equal is used with equal values.

interview.question: Explain the three taint effects.
interview.answer: NoSchedule prevents new pods from being scheduled onto the node unless they tolerate the taint. PreferNoSchedule is a softer preference, while NoExecute also evicts running pods that do not tolerate it.
interview.followUp: What controls delayed eviction? A NoExecute toleration can set tolerationSeconds; when omitted, the pod tolerates the taint indefinitely.

interview.question: How do you configure a workload to use a tainted node?
interview.answer: Apply a taint with kubectl, for example `kubectl taint nodes node1 key1=value1:NoSchedule`. Add the corresponding key, operator, value, and effect under the pod's `spec.tolerations`.
interview.followUp: How would you reserve a node rather than merely permit access? Combine the toleration with another placement constraint, because tolerations alone do not select a node.

keyPoints: Attach one or more taints to a node to repel pods lacking the corresponding tolerations.
Declare tolerations in the PodSpec, rather than on the node.
A match requires identical taint and toleration keys and effects before the operator/value rule is evaluated.
NoSchedule blocks newly scheduled pods that lack a matching toleration.
gotchas: A toleration makes a pod eligible for a tainted node, but it does not ensure that the scheduler will place the pod there.
Using an empty toleration is broad: it can match every taint, so prefer a narrowly scoped key, value, and effect when reserving nodes.
For Exists matching, omit value; supplying one makes the toleration invalid for that matching rule.
